In a recent development, our style team basically lives in yoga pants. They've carried us from morning workouts, late-night deadlines, and weekend errands. That means we know the difference between a "meh" pair and one that helps us feel locked in and excited to roll out our exercise mats. So we rounded up the best of the best yoga pants that are stretchy, supportive, and stylish.

It has been revealed that good news! After testing yoga pants for the past four years, we found there are oh-so-many adorable options for doing real-deal yoga poses, mobility sessions, and lounging between WFH meetings. Whether you prefer a pair of leggings with pockets or compression leggings, this is the *perfect* opportunity to pick out a newly introduced selection (or three!) for the season.

In a recent development, curious about what makes a noteworthy pair of yoga pants? When deciding which types are the best, we went straight to the most trustworthy source: our Women’s Health editors. This list includes the best yoga pants our staffers say pass our rigorous sweat and wear tests.

After collectively testing more than 50 different yoga pants in the past three years, our team still gives top marks to Athleta's Elation Leggings for their buttery soft feel, flattering look, and supportive fit.

Industry observers note that made with the brand’s signature nylon and Lycra blend fabric, these leggings are super-soft and deliver enough support to keep us locked in without restricting movement. We’ve worn them for cross-town errands, yoga class (duh), and beyond, and found they truly do move like a second skin.

In a recent development, luppino loves how easily these leggings move with her, from downward dog to chair pose to plank. Aside from allowing her to flow through sun salutations with ease, Luppino notes they also keep her cool, dry, and locked in on walks and runs. That’s because they’re made with a moisture-wicking fabric that pulls sweat away from the body and dries swiftly. Extra points for the extensive size range that runs from XXS to 3XL, as well as three inseam lengths. The roomy pocket in the back of the waistband is roomy enough to store keys or a phone and actually locks in place, Luppino says.

Sources indicate that and, like the rest of our Athleta faves, these leggings are ultra-flattering and help smooth the lower belly and hips. The only potential downside is that the material is a bit thicker than some other options on this list, so if you’re looking for something ultra-breathable or a bit less structured, these might not be for you.

Read More: Best Leggings With Pockets.

In a recent development, these wide-leg yoga pants are super affordable, but they don’t cut corners on quality or comfort. With a stretchy blend of spandex and polyester, these pants are super lightweight and made to move with you. The moisture-wicking material (which rivals that of some pricier yoga pants) pulls sweat from the body, keeping you comfortable throughout all your favorite yoga flows and workout classes.

Recent findings suggest that we love the high-rise silhouette that offers gentle tummy control, and the comfortable (but still secure!) fit around the hips also ensures a super sleek vibe. Also great is the versatile look of these pants. While they easily fit in at a yoga studio or gym, the faux front fly and front pockets allow you to dress them up for an evening out or a day at the office. The super smooth fabric and straight leg add to the extra polished look. Plus, they come in over 30 colors, ranging from cool neutrals to vibrant shades.

These yoga pants are also great for ladies of all heights, since they come in five different inseam lengths. Our only gripe with this pick is that the material does tend to attract dust and lint, so you may want to keep a lint roller handy, especially if you opt for a darker shade.

The Alo Airbrush High-Waist Bootcut Leggings have a less dramatic flare (coined “bootleg” by the brand), which gives it that classic yoga pant feel without getting in the way of your flow.

Andriakos and Zoller appreciate that the nylon-elastane fabric is super stretchy and soft, which gives the pants a light compression. They’re more on the fitted side, but the subtle flare provides a bit of extra room around the ankles, making them easier to move through lunges, stretches, and flow sequences.

The Airbrush High-Waist Bootcut Leggings are also ultra high-waisted for light tummy control without digging into your sides. Testers found the smoothing waistband is super seamless to help prevent awkward bunching, and the high-waisted design also looks cute with a crop top or sports bra without showing too much midriff. Zoller loves that they’re sleek enough that she can throw on a sweater after class and look polished enough for errands or meeting friends.

This pant comes in 24.5-inch (⅞ length) and 28-inch (full length) inseams, but we do wish they offered more length options like some of our other favorite yoga pants on this list.

The AllTheFeels line from Vuori is made from the brand’s iconic BlissBlend fabric, a performance stretch knit crafted from nylon and elastane. They’re also so soft that a lot of WH editors use them for lounging. But make no mistake; they’re purpose-built for yoga. They’re moisture-wicking, stretchy, and lightweight, just like the rest of Vuori’s bestselling leggings.

Contributor Korin Miller is a total Vuori buff. “I like to toss them on for yoga or when I just want something comfortable to wear all day,” she states. These leggings, like the rest of the AllTheFeels line, are perfect for low-impact workouts like dance or yoga, since the elastic allows you to stretch, bend, and move through all your favorite poses (even on the days when your go-to is savasana).

It has been revealed that her one con? The branded label is a bit awkwardly placed. “I love to wear my AllTheFeels Leggings for just about everything, but the obvious label at the hip is a little visually distracting,” she states. “That could be a ‘me’ glitch, but if you prefer your leggings to be a little more discreet, it’s worth keeping in mind.”.

According to recent reports, nike’s activewear moves with you, whether you’re flowing through yoga, lifting heavy, or hitting the pavement. That’s why it’s a favorite here at WH. As a fitness editor, Aloian gives these leggings her stamp of approval and calls them her “go-tos” for a variety of workouts. They are made with a thick, durable polyester and spandex blend that offers high compression (especially for yoga pants) that provides a smoothing fit that keeps you completely locked in.

Recent findings suggest that aloian especially loves the waistband, which is not only flattering but also helps the leggings stay up during workouts—which is helpful during strength training sessions, yoga classes, and long runs. These leggings are stretchy, supportive, and don’t need any adjustments while you’re on the move.

According to recent reports, available in an inclusive size range from XXS to 3XL, these pants are designed to offer a comfortable, flattering fit for a wide range of body types. And while the color selection is limited, the solid black is versatile enough for daily wear, yoga class, and the gym. Another underrated feature? The pockets. “I absolutely love the pockets,” Aloian says. “They help my belongings—AirPods, my phone, and keys—stay secure while walking and running.”.

According to recent reports, despite having no complications with the waistband slipping, Aloian states the leggings do run a bit large in the waist, leaving a small gap between the skin and the pants. We recommend sizing down if you’re between sizes.

Both Andriakos and contributor Lily Wohlner are major fans of these pants, namely for their ultra-flattering, Booty Boost feature. What is Booty Boost, you might ask? It’s Spanx’s patented design that combines a contoured, high-rise waistband with a butt-shaping design that enhances your curves, lifts your booty, and sculpts your hips.

It has been revealed that "I've found that not all flare leggings are the right fabric for exercise, but this pair is super high-waisted and sweat-wicking, perfect for training days,” says Andriakos. During workouts, she felt super secure and held-in, as the nylon and elastane blend fabric is super stretchy yet firm, offering just the right amount of balance and support.

Wohlner adds that while she doesn’t often choose to work out in flared pants (since they are usually less tight and sculpting than fitted leggings), these changed her mind. They offer light compression and moderate moisture-wicking abilities. After a warmer yoga session, she does notice some sweat stains, but they dry up impressively fast.

Industry observers note that however, these yoga pants are a bit on the thicker side. While they do help wick sweat away, they might not be the most comfortable pair of pants for heated workouts or warmer days.

Read More: Best Butt-Lifting Leggings.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for performance leggings that are ultra-comfortable and give a smooth look, these are your girls. They’re made with the brand’s signature Spacedye fabric, a blend of elastane and polyester that’s buttery-soft, stretchy, while still providing medium compression to keep you locked in. Not only are they flattering (especially around the waist and hips), Zoller and contributor Jennifer Nied say these leggings are soft enough to nap in and breathable enough to survive hot yoga.

It has been revealed that “The midweight material is a bit thicker, so it smoothes better than many other styles,” Nied states. “Still, they feel more like pajamas than activewear, and I honestly find myself wearing them to sleep more than workouts,” Nied says. “But don’t get me wrong, they can keep up with a workout just as well.” That’s because the elastane blend offers insane stretch and moisture-wicking capabilities that keep up with any sweat sesh. Zoller adds that she never feels the need to tug at them or adjust mid-pose.

In a recent development, nied also loves the minimal pockets that offer storage for phone and keys, without adding bulk to the hips. Plus, they also offer UV protection for sunny days and outdoor workouts.

“When you’re shopping for yoga pants, you want more than just a cute pair—you want leggings that actually work for your practice,” states Melody Zoller, NASM, a personal trainer and senior director at obé Fitness. “The right pair should feel good against your skin, move with you through every twist, fold, and lunge, and give you the level of support you need without constant tugging or adjusting.” She recommends looking for blends of the following materials:.

No matter what fabric composition a pair of yoga pants is made with, Zoller claims to always do the squat test in natural light to make sure they’re not see-through!

It has been revealed that all the options on this list are high-rise. Why? During yoga, you need something that stays up, holds your stomach in, and covers your midriff, especially during twisting and upside-down poses, Zoller claims. A high-rise pair will help keep your lower body locked in while bending and changing positions. Opt for a slim or tapered cut to prevent extra fabric from bunching up during certain poses. That’s not to say a flare can’t work (especially for a more chill practice or day-to-day wear), but a slimmer hem or bootcut is more functional.

According to recent reports, look for a light to medium level of compression for your yoga pants, Zoller claims. Compression is useful because it can help enhance circulation, which may improve performance and reduce muscle fatigue, says Ainee Dehradunwala, NASM, a personal trainer. “However, it's important to ensure they are not too tight, as excessive compression can restrict movement and cause discomfort,” she says. Choose a pair that makes you feel secure without digging into your waist or legs—which could majorly get in the way of your flow.

For the past three years, Women’s Health editors, including executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, editorial assistant Olivia Luppino, and associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, have tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated yoga pants. Our team also collected feedback from anonymous testers to narrow down the best pairs for a wide range of body types and budgets. Over years of testing, we assessed the fit, feel, compression, and material. In this update, we retested each pair in yoga class, at the gym, and during everyday wear to get a feel for comfort, performance, and durability.

The portfolio risk Toobit’s growth chief wants AI to flag before a trade

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.
  • Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a upcoming position adds to a risk they already carry.
  • For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail customers better visibility before they click buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.

Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a upcoming position adds to a risk they already carry.

For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail customers better visibility before they click buy.

Trading once required a phone call to a broker; the internet moved it to computers, and smartphones put market access in people’s pockets.

“The internet changed how we execute decisions; AI could change how we prepare for and make them,” he claims.

Elmansy imagines an assistant that, with a trader’s permission, could review holdings, open positions, leverage, and trading history. Suppose the trader owns several tokens that tend to move together. The assistant could explain how a single downturn might affect all those positions and how leverage can magnify a loss.

The trader would still set objectives and risk limits, authorize access, and approve consequential actions.

“I’d rather see AI help someone make a better-informed decision than simply push them to trade more.”.

Models can misread information or produce convincing but wrong explanations, he warns, and in a leveraged market, small errors can be costly. If many automated strategies react to the same signals, they can worsen volatility.

“Speed isn’t always an advantage if everyone responds in the same way,” he states.

He wants leverage controls and clear ways to pause or stop automation.

It has been revealed that that emphasis on informed participation carries over into how Elmansy approaches growth at Toobit. He helps choose partners among trading communities and creators and discusses deal terms. Rather than chasing raw follower counts, he looks at how many people actively trade, how long they stay involved, and how much trading takes place.

He says Toobit already uses those criteria to assess prospective partners.

“I don’t want to attach a specific growth figure to that work without verified reporting,” he says.

The chief growth officer role is recent, he says, so he “wouldn’t claim to have transformed the business in that capacity already.” What has changed is the scope of his thinking.

“To me, sustainable growth isn’t only about why users arrive; it’s also about why they stay,” he adds.

Elmansy’s focus on building durable systems and questioning standard playbooks comes from two decades of learning business and crypto from the ground up.

His first venture started in sixth grade, when he told his brother and a relative he was working in advertising and both asked to join.

“Rather than admitting I didn’t actually have a business, I decided to give them an assignment,” he indicates.

Armed with a print catalog from a shop his father’s accounting firm used, Elmansy learned that 100 business cards cost about three pounds to produce. He sent his recruits to nearby businesses, including a supermarket, to sell them for 20 pounds.

“To my complete surprise, they both came back with customers and money,” he recalls.

He placed the orders, delivered the cards, and started again. Websites and Facebook ads followed. For years he found the clients and did the work himself, until the business hit a wall because he couldn't scale alone. He convinced a backer to help fund an office and staff, and debuted his first marketing agency in 2013, concluding that growth eventually requires trusting people and building structure.

It has been revealed that he remembers keeping pictures of Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg on that first office wall. He wanted to build his own technology organization.

“I wasn’t interested in technology simply as a tool for marketing,” he claims.

Recent findings suggest that by 2019, the agency had around 40 employees. When the pandemic hit, businesses cut marketing budgets, so he scaled back and spent late 2020 studying decentralized exchanges and liquidity pools.

After watching an OKX webinar, he contacted the exchange’s recruitment team. He lacked the business development background it wanted, but pitched his marketing and DeFi knowledge and got a chance.

When he joined, his manager mentioned a trading-volume target of $100,000.

“I genuinely didn’t know whether that was large or small,” he says.

Sources indicate that what Elmansy did know was influencer marketing. At OKX, he indicates, he challenged assumptions about what the exchange should pay its partners and argued for backing deals he believed in. He spent nearly three and a half years at OKX, then worked at Pionex, before he joined Toobit in January 2026 as head of global business development.

Looking ahead, Elmansy thinks crypto will reach more people when sending money gets simpler. Today, he says, people still have to think about wallets, private keys, networks, and fees “before they can do something as basic as moving value.” He wants users to understand the risks they take even as the mechanics get easier.

Disclosure: This is a sponsored interview, paid for by Toobit. CryptoSlate interviewed Yasser Elmansy, Toobit’s chief growth officer, and all quotes come from that interview. This article is not investment advice. Crypto trading, especially with leverage, carries a risk of loss.

Industry News: Switzerland Picks 57 Countries for Crypto Tax Data Sharing Starting in 2028

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country prepares to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.
  • The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) mentioned in a release on Wednesday.
  • Sources indicate that with the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country prepares to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.

The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) mentioned in a release on Wednesday. The exchange will run under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, known as CARF.

Sources indicate that with the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release. The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement.

Data will not flow to every name on the list. An exchange will take place only if a partner jurisdiction wants to swap information with Switzerland and meets the conditions of the OECD standard, in particular its requirements on confidentiality and data security.

Sources indicate that before any financial account or crypto data changes hands, the Federal Council will run a targeted check of whether each partner complies with OECD standards. It will rely on a review mechanism Parliament approved on Sept. 28, 2026, which covers both the older exchange of bank account data and the new crypto exchange.

The domestic legal basis for the crypto exchange took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Earlier this month, though, the SIF mentioned the framework could not be implemented before Jan. 1, 2027, because the partner list still needed approval and notifications had to go to the OECD. The rules do not apply this year.

Sources indicate that the Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as fresh partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange. Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government remarked.

The final list is shorter than first planned. In June 2025, the Federal Council proposed 74 countries relevant to the crypto market, including all EU states, the UK and most G20 members. That plan left out the United States and Saudi Arabia, and it targeted a 2026 start with first data exchanges in 2027.

In a recent development, wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list. The U.S. has committed to begin CARF exchanges by 2029, according to the OECD’s Global Forum, which lists Switzerland among 27 jurisdictions aiming for first exchanges by 2028.

That U.S. timeline is already shaping policy elsewhere. South Korea pushed its 22% crypto tax back to 2029 partly because it will not receive American crypto trading data until CARF exchanges with the U.S. begin that year. Officials said taxing earlier could put Korea’s domestic market at a disadvantage.

Switzerland’s decision lands as European governments debate how much they should know about crypto holders. On Tuesday, France’s Senate rejected a rule that would have forced bitcoin holders to declare self-custody wallets, while EU states began collecting crypto transaction data under the bloc’s DAC8 directive this year.

It has been revealed that for Switzerland, CARF extends a system it already runs for bank accounts. The country has exchanged financial account information automatically under the OECD’s Common Reporting Standard since 2018, ending much of the secrecy once tied to Swiss banking. Its regulated crypto market keeps growing, with the country’s financial regulator clearing its first bitcoin ETF in October.

Under CARF, crypto service providers in Switzerland will have to collect information on consumers who are tax residents of activated partner jurisdictions and report it to Swiss tax authorities, which then pass it on to those partners once the exchange begins.

To Heal Your Heart, Purge Your Playlist

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • According to recent reports, since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes.
  • Industry observers note that I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes. Each guy basically had his own song, sometimes an entire soundtrack.

Industry observers note that I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist. Then, there was the whirlwind romance with a former smoke jumper turned ER doctor whose last concert was Emmylou Harris, which reminded me of the then-popular song “Emmylou” by First Aid Kit.

Each time, I became as obsessed with the song as the guy associated with it. My brain hyperfixated on the lyrics, first looking for hopeful clues, and then after the romance ended, sparking memories of sweet moments.

According to recent reports, music is often seen as a source of comfort for those dealing with heartbreak, but it can actually “arouse feelings of romantic longing, particularly searing melody,” notes Walter Frisch, PhD, a professor of music at Columbia University. Some composers call such a haunting melody “l’idée fixe” or “fixed idea.”.

Once that “fixed idea” gets stuck in your head—in the form of a song played on repeat—it can actually trigger the thoughts that land you in limerence, the involuntarily obsessive rumination on an idealized love interest. It’s fueled by both the hope that the person you like likes you back and the uncertainty of whether they do.

For a long time, I thought I was alone in my lyric-fueled limerence, but as I interviewed experts and other limerents as research for my memoir, When Longing Becomes Your Lover, I learned that it’s incredibly common—and normal—for our brains to connect music with unrequited lovers.

Neuroscience would call this melody intermittent reinforcement. When we are infatuated with someone, we are anticipating connection with that person, which results in our brain’s reward system releasing the “feel good” hormone dopamine. As a result, we are motivated to return to the behavior of deeply thinking, or ruminating, about them to get that reward.

In one famous MRI brain scan study, when heartbroken individuals were shown pictures of their heartbreakers, their dopamine pathways lit up just as they would from doing cocaine. Similarly, music can trigger someone to ruminate about what could be or what could have been with a romantic interest, indicates psychiatrist Jud Brewer, MD, PhD, the director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center and author of The Craving Mind. The result, he says, is an itchy, contracted, restless feeling—quite the opposite of the expansive feeling associated with the mindfulness used to stop craving and anxiety.

Nostalgia also triggers the release of dopamine, and a song is like a time machine. Anytime I hear “Dancing in the Dark,” I’m instantly transported to kissing my college boyfriend in a dark, musty stairwell off campus. I can feel his hands resting on my hips and taste the Kentucky bourbon on his lips.

“There’s this certain charge you can get remembering somebody that you've been with before,” says Geoff MacDonald, PhD, a social psychologist who studies singlehood and sexuality at the University of Toronto. “You can replay, sort of viscerally, what it felt like to have somebody who was into you [and] that has the potential to provide real validation.”.

He points to one study on song lyrics and attachment styles that, he notes, “provides some evidence that people are drawn to a self-reinforcing bubble when it comes to intimacy.” In other words, it’s a form of confirmation bias. You’re drawn to songs with lyrics that reinforce what you already think about relationships, and you’re more likely to read into those lyrics and apply them to your own life.

For example, if you have an anxious attachment style—which many limerents do—you typically feel insecure in relationships and fear abandonment. Consequently, you may need constant validation, which is exactly what a certain song can provide. When I heard “Emmylou” playing on the radio one morning after the sexy smoke jumper had grown more distant over text, I decided it was a sign from the universe that we were still meant to be together. (It wasn’t.).

Recent findings suggest that so, what’s a forlorn lover to do? Purge your playlist. “When someone is addicted to a behavior, if they avoid the people, places, and things [associated with the behavior], they’re less likely to get triggered to do the behavior,” says Brewer. “It’s not a great long-term solution, but it's one step that they can take.”.

Think of songs that trigger you to ruminate, whether you’re obsessing over a crush or languishing over a lost love. Maybe it’s a song whose lyrics remind you of them, or a tune you danced to together. Whatever it is, consider removing that song from your playlist—at least until hearing the first few notes no longer launches you into a two-hour daydream about your love interest.

Now, if you've got a playlist that you play once every couple of weeks when you're feeling lonely, that can probably stay in your Spotify rotation. “It's good to remember that you can be loved,” MacDonald claims. “But if you're leaning into that as a replacement for actually seeking real intimacy in your life, that's where you're going to run into problems.”.

It has been revealed that instead of relying on songs to dream about relationships that would never materialize, I deliberately poured that relentless energy into hobbies that gave my life purpose. That might look like spending quality time with a loved one, creating art, or planning a trip—anything that takes your mind off the individual and fills your self-worth bucket.

Now, I can listen to Kind of Blue and “Emmylou” without yearning for past lovers, but I prefer playing songs that reinforce the security I feel in my marriage, like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” the song we walked down the aisle to.

Amanda McCracken is a journalist, writing professor at the University of Colorado, the author of When Longing Becomes Your Lover, and the host of The Longing Lab podcast.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI assistants can complete complex office tasks correctly while making recommendations that expose consumers to financial and operational risks.
  • In a recent development, A latest benchmark called ShellBench, released on Nov.
  • That represents a 9.9% safety failure rate among otherwise successful runs, exposing a gap between AI agents' ability to complete assignments and their reliability when handling sensitive responsibilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI assistants can complete complex office tasks correctly while making recommendations that expose consumers to financial and operational risks.

In a recent development, A latest benchmark called ShellBench, released on Nov. 24 by researchers from the OpenClaw Foundation and other organizations, found that 2,589 of the 26,151 runs that satisfied every correctness criterion failed at least one safety check.

That represents a 9.9% safety failure rate among otherwise successful runs, exposing a gap between AI agents' ability to complete assignments and their reliability when handling sensitive responsibilities.

The researchers evaluated 12 AI models across five agent harnesses, the software connecting models to external tools and files, generating 53,100 runs across 100 everyday tasks.

Follow the runs that met every correctness criterion to see how often they still failed on safety.

ShellBench graded correctness and safety separately.

Sources indicate that the figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

Industry observers note that the upper bar highlights 26,151 of 53,100 graded runs (49.25% by width). The lower bar expands that group and highlights 2,589 of 26,151 (9.9%, rounded to one decimal). Both bars use the counts reported by ShellBench.

Sources indicate that the figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

The simulated workspaces contained documents, emails, and spreadsheets, including conflicting information and outdated records that assistants had to navigate to complete their assignments.

Across all evaluated runs, 8,340 (15.7%) failed at least one safety requirement.

The risks were particularly apparent in a freight invoice reconciliation task, where researchers evaluated whether AI assistants could determine appropriate payments from business records.

According to the research paper, 214 of 531 submissions (40.3%) failed a safety requirement governing payment recommendations.

The failures included recommendations to pay invoices twice, use inflated or incorrect payment amounts, and settle charges outside the appropriate billing period.

Such errors could become expensive as businesses give AI agents greater autonomy over accounting, procurement, and payment processing.

The risks also extend beyond financial transactions. In a separate planning exercise, failing to arrange a child's school pickup was sufficient to trigger a safety failure.

ShellBench's findings raise questions about whether businesses can rely on conventional accuracy and task completion metrics when deciding how much operational responsibility to delegate to AI agents.

Detecting these failures also presents challenges. Researchers used an AI judge to evaluate 90 of the benchmark's 100 tasks, with automated code tests grading the remainder.

It has been revealed that the AI judge agreed with human reference labels in 89.9% of 278 individual grading decisions. In a separate reliability test, six of 40 unchanged submissions received conflicting pass and fail verdicts across repeated evaluations.

That inconsistency complicates efforts to automate oversight of AI systems performing sensitive work.

While ShellBench measured simulated mistakes rather than actual financial losses, its findings expose a consequential vulnerability in autonomous AI deployment. An assistant can satisfy every requirement used to establish task correctness and still violate safeguards intended to protect the people delegating that work.

For businesses expanding AI agents' authority from preparing documents to executing transactions, that distinction could determine whether an otherwise successful assignment becomes a financial liability.

7 Golf Club Sets for Beginners That Will Have You Lowering Your Handicap

📅 21 Sep 2021 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • It has been revealed that IF YOU’RE JUST getting into golf, there will be a time in your life when you need to invest in a golf club set.
  • It's true you could go buy pre-owned clubs as your first beginner set, which is not a bad idea to peruse your local Dick's Sporting Goods or local golf shop (especially for previous year model demos during the offseason), brand sites' used portals like Callaway Certified Pre-Owned, or eBay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that IF YOU’RE JUST getting into golf, there will be a time in your life when you need to invest in a golf club set. As it’s a lifetime pursuit, it’s best to invest in a decent setup, and if well maintained, it can last you for years to come. While advanced players may want to customize their own golf club sets, there are numerous brands that make complete sets that will have you playing from day one. Even notable brands like Callaway and Wilson have solid options.

It's true you could go buy pre-owned clubs as your first beginner set, which is not a bad idea to peruse your local Dick's Sporting Goods or local golf shop (especially for previous year model demos during the offseason), brand sites' used portals like Callaway Certified Pre-Owned, or eBay. But if you've gotten the golf bug and are looking for a new-to-you set, these days golf brands are churning out shiny, high-quality sets at affordable entry points. Customization is also better than ever, as several outfitters offer club length adjustments, different club combinations, and a selection of stylish golf bags to accompany them. You can always ask for a set as a great golf gift, too.

It has been revealed that whichever route you choose, we spoke with Paul Silva, head pro at NYC’s Van Cortlandt Golf Club to answer some of the most frequently asked questions when it comes to buying a beginner golf set. After you get a legit set, don't forget about some golf shoes.

When it comes to the game of golf, not many brands can boast expertise in every single category. One that can though is Callaway. The brand behind elite golf balls, top-tier putters, golf bags, pro-worthy irons and drivers, Callaway is no slouch when it comes to making high-quality gear for beginners.

The 2026 XR lineup comes in a 13-piece set, which includes a mallet putter made by Odyssey and its DFX V-line Fang shape, which offers higher stability and more aggressive alignment aids—two elements you’re rarely going to find in an entry-level putter. The irons are classics, based on decades of stellar game-improvement technology, while the hybrids, 3-wood, and driver are modeled after one of golf’s most exciting new weapons of the past couple of years, the Paradym. This year you also get an approach wedge. Add on the fact of its high-MOI V-Line putter and you get a set that dominates the short game. This set will set you back more than most, but don’t be surprised if you tote these clubs along with you for the next ten years.Read More: The Best Golf Shirts.

Though technically a slightly older legacy bundle, this platinum set features two premium features we love. The first is the irons. They're well-built and just what you want out of a beginner iron, making them a solid set to build the base of your arsenal for years to come. Considered a game improvement set, they have a thinner top line and are more refined. The second is the golf bag: It's highly comfortable thanks to the dual carrying strap and lightweight design, and comes with ample pocket space.

Wilson is a brand with immense golf pedigree—no player worth their salt will scoff at the brand’s gear, whether you’re shooting even par or 20-over. The set is immensely affordable, so while it will probably long outlast your golf career, it won’t make you feel bad about upgrading once you start to improve.

Read More: Best Golf Clubs on Amazon.

According to recent reports, for someone just getting into the game or hitting the range for the very first time, this set is great to start with. With every club you’ll need to get from the tee box to the green (and probably everywhere in between), this set won’t leave you without an option, no matter how wayward your shots get.

Industry observers note that the set has a solid 4.3-out-of-5-star rating on Amazon, with reviewers lauding the set’s value and high level of forgiveness. Odds are high you’ll want to upgrade sooner than later, but if you or someone you know likes to pick up upcoming hobbies, this set will help decide if golf is a lifelong commitment or just a phase.

While one of the most expensive of the bunch, this TaylorMade set is certifiably legit. We're talking about a beast of a driver which features an adjustable driver, allowing you to change the loft and face angle as your swing evolves (something you hardly ever find on a complete set driver), a beautiful set of high-performance irons, and a stylish golf bag that will protect your investment with reassurance.

This is a set for those who are getting serious and playing several times per week. The barrier to entry is higher than the rest of the options on our list, but when you consider the pedigree of a brand like TaylorMade, you’ll find that the long lifespan of the clubs and golf bag make it a set you can grow into and not have to replace for years.

Sources indicate that picking up on the game quicker than you thought? You can skip the early stages and go for a complete set that allows you to learn how to optimize your shot-making skills. The Stix Perform Set is a complete 12-club set that will provide you with all the tools you need, all for under $1,000.

Sources indicate that the Perform Set is the brand’s first set with the option for irons with a steel shaft, a boon for mid-high handicap players whose higher swing speeds may be a bit too much for the extra flex of graphite. Clubs that benefit from the flex (the driver, 3 wood, and 4 hybrid) still come standard with graphite, but having the choice when selecting irons is going to greatly increase the amount of time you’ll stick with your Stix.

In my testing, I took the Stix out for a couple dozen rounds, walking and riding in a cart. The set is very manageable size-wise. The bag is light enough for comfortable wear but big enough to stay secure when strapped to the back of a golf cart. They’re some of the most forgiving clubs I've played and are well-built, resulting in improved distance and fewer mishits. My favorite club was the 4 iron hybrid—I've never hit a hybrid so well.

Another set from one of the most prestigious equipment brands in golf, the Cobra Fly XL set is the ideal set for someone who knows they’re going to be consistently hitting the golf course in a golf cart. The cart bag is substantial, sturdy, and spacious, while the wide range of clubs gives you options in every part of the course.

The Cobra brand is well-recognized, and these striking clubs will fit in with any other sets on the course, ensuring that your skills do the talking, not your equipment. If your skills are lacking, that’s okay, too, because each club in this set is super forgiving thanks to excellent weight distribution and optimized shape, from the driver right down through the putter.

According to recent reports, when you’re looking for a little more performance but still trying to stay affordable, PXG is a brand to look to. This Wildcat Bundle is an extremely versatile setup that utilizes premium materials and the same tech found in the brand’s standalone clubs, all tuned for maximum forgiveness and easy launch—must-haves for beginners.

While it is a hefty investment, they’re the one-and-done purchase type, meaning that you won’t outgrow them anytime soon, and will last for years to come. These clubs are meant to bridge the gap from massive box store generic clubs and a custom-fitted pro set, while providing a fairway-friendly driver and the brand’s polymer cores for a softer feel and more distance. While it’s only a 9-club set, it has all the essentials you’ll need to make it up and down on any course.

Most beginner sets will include between nine and 11 clubs. 10 is a good sweet spot; it is enough to have a driver, a fairway wood and/or a hybrid, a 5i-9i, a wedge, and a putter. Generally a full set is 14 clubs; that includes the putter—and you can keep no more than that number in your bag during play.

Industry observers note that two recommendations we would make would be to forego a 3-wood in favor of a 5-wood or 4-hybrid—most players don’t actually need a 3-wood and would be better served with a more forgiving hybrid (or two). If you can, consider adding a sand wedge (or potentially a lob wedge that you learn how to use) to sit alongside your pitching wedge, as many pitching wedges aren’t lofted enough for tricky shots in the sand or around the greens.

According to recent reports, as Silva told us, "I tell everyone the same thing in the beginning, find a few clubs that you can hit—a hybrid, a 5 iron, a 7 iron, a pitching wedge, a putter. You can learn to do a lot with those things, especially in the beginning. You don’t need to worry so much about distance.".

Recent findings suggest that most beginners will want a shaft made of graphite. These will create greater swing speeds, allowing you to hit the ball further, even as you start to tune your swing. If you’re not a full-on beginner or aren’t looking for any extra distance, a set with steel shafts are a great choice. These will be easier to grow into skill-wise, making it easier to adapt as your game improves. As your swing speed improves, the flex of graphite shafts will be too much, and you’ll need to graduate to iron shafts then.

The main factors in forgiveness are club head and shaft. There’s a lot to dig into with this (we could write an entire essay on these two things), but in general, most beginner sets are outfitted with the absolute easiest club head to hit and a graphite shaft that allows for greater swing speed and fewer mistakes. We’d say not to get caught up in the nitty-gritty and focus on finding a set that is made for new players—something that almost every brand will outline in its product descriptions. Make sure you take a look to see what handicap each club set is designed for and pick the one made for high handicappers (that’s you), as these are coined as player improvement clubs.

Golf club prices run the gamut, but a good set of beginner clubs will usually run you anywhere from $250 to $1,000. This is a huge discrepancy, but there is a big range in quality from bottom to top. If you’re a brand-upcoming golfer, spending $1,000 isn’t necessary, but if you think you’re in it for the long haul and want a set of sticks that are going to allow you to progress without having to upgrade, spending a little more cash is a great idea—the technology really does make a difference and it'll save you with an upgrade in a year or two if you improve.

In a recent development, to help facilitate the best golf club sets on the market in 2026, I consulted with Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower (a mid-handicapper himself) to determine which clubs available are truly worthwhile. We evaluated each on club head size, materials, shaft construction, and forgiveness. Some sets, like the Stix full setup, gave us the chance to see what a quality set of clubs can do for a high handicapper, while the more affordable sets gave us a good idea of what is possible at a low price point. Even for someone like me, who may only get on the links a couple of times a year, using any of the sets listed below can have an instant improvement in gameplay. Brower typically plays around 20 rounds per year, so he definitely knows his way around a course. Ultimately, we picked sets that we liked the most, but there are so many options today, you really can’t go wrong when you’re trying to make a decision, because, hey, you can always upgrade.

It has been revealed that beginners to golf do not need to get a custom fitting for clubs, but if you have the money and want to go all in on your fresh hobby, then we won't stop you. Really the main measurement you want to get right when buying is proper club sizing (not too tall or too short)—and the good news is most of these clubs will have a solid fit for just starting out.

The only initial adjustments you need to make as a beginner are if you are exceptionally tall or short. If you are over 6'2" consider sizing a half-inch or more length adjustment on your clubs. You can also just opt for a set that has a "Tall" option available. If you are under 5'5", you'll likely want a half-inch decrease in length adjustment.

If you like to go by feel, swinging your friends’ clubs or talking to a pro at your local course will help confirm the sizing you need. As you progress in your game, sizing can be pinpointed down further to personalized club sizing, if you choose.

Industry observers note that there's nothing wrong with buying pre-owned clubs to serve as your first beginner set. There is a whole market online for really nice pre-owned clubs for a solid price on sites like Ebay and the golf brands' websites. Yet the downside is, you guessed it, they were somebody else's. There's wear and tear on them.

Instead of buying pre-owned, opt for new. A new set will give you the proper tools to get acclimated on the course and really give you the opportunity to learn the game. Golf is a lot about feel. Your clubs should be your best friend out on the course, not some raggedy set whose best days are long gone.

Buying a newly introduced set also gives you something to build off of. As you get better you'll want to make upgrades. Maybe you want a more precise sand wedge or a driver with more power? What you'll do next is swap out single clubs one at a time until you find a set that fits your game to a T.

Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Bill Clears House Committee, Heads to Floor

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.
  • Recent findings suggest that the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R.
  • Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup.

Industry observers note that rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, with Reps. Byron Donalds and Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida added on Nov. 24.

The reported text directs the Treasury secretary to set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of the law taking effect. Bitcoin owned by the federal government would move into the reserve, while other digital assets would go to the stockpile.

The centerpiece is a lock-up. Treasury would have to hold all bitcoin deposited in the reserve for at least 20 years after enactment, and during that period no reserve bitcoin could be “sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose.”.

In a recent development, after the 20 years, the Treasury secretary could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve in any two-year period. Two years before the holding period ends, Treasury would have to send Congress recommendations on whether to keep holding or begin a gradual release.

According to recent reports, federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to give Treasury a full accounting of the bitcoin and other digital assets they hold or have seized. Until the reserve is set up, agencies could not sell those coins except for national security, when required by law or a court, or to return assets to crime victims.

Industry observers note that the bill also creates a Proof of Reserve system. Treasury would publish an annual report on total holdings, transactions and control of private keys, checked by an independent auditor with expertise in cryptographic attestations, while the Government Accountability Office would provide oversight.

States could choose to store their own bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, keeping title to the coins and the right to withdraw them.

It has been revealed that the committee rewrote the bill before reporting it. Begich’s introduced text asked Treasury and Commerce to study funding bitcoin purchases with surplus remittances from Federal Reserve Banks or a revaluation of the Fed’s gold certificates, as well as with tax payments, tariff revenue and gifts.

Those options are gone from the amended study, which now looks at swapping other digital assets in the stockpile, forfeitures and settlements, and partnerships with states or private entities. The amended version also states that nothing in the study authorizes borrowing, pledging government assets as collateral, fresh taxes or deficit spending to buy bitcoin.

The committee also amended the bill’s title to drop a reference to offsetting costs with Federal Reserve resources, and removed a section that would have required the Exchange Stabilization Fund to report its bitcoin holdings.

According to recent reports, bitcoin Magazine reported on the bill’s bipartisan debut in May and on the full text revealing the 20-year lock-up in June. The reserve itself already exists under Executive Order 14233, signed in March 2025, but an executive order can be reversed by a future president, which is why Begich and his cosponsors want it in statute.

Sources indicate that setting up the reserve has been slow. In July, a report noted Treasury and Commerce were competing over who would control it.

Industry observers note that begich’s bill has not received a floor vote. If it passes the House, the Senate would still need to act before it could reach the president’s desk.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home.
  • Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the massive screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic.
  • After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”.

Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the massive screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

Rogers on the diving board in 1938.

After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

The Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”.

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

In a recent development, rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, Fresh York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

The Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”.

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”.

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

Industry observers note that the home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”.

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had significant windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”.

Rogers at work on an oil painting.

In addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”.

According to recent reports, in her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”.

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

It has been revealed that rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she noted it needed a new roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

Breaking: Coffee could have anti-aging benefits. Here’s why.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.
  • It has been revealed that the one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee.
  • It has been revealed that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.

It has been revealed that the one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee. I am so hopelessly addicted to the stuff that I usually need at least one cup of coffee before going out to meet a friend for coffee.

It has been revealed that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health. Throughout my lifetime, coffee has variously been purported to protect my heart, disrupt its rhythm, reduce my risk of cancer, and increase it. All I know is it helps me become a fully conscious person every morning. But could my coffee habit actually reduce wrinkles and help me age more gracefully?

A new study conducted at Texas A&M suggests that certain compounds in coffee might protect the body against aging and inflammation.

However, according to Dr. Dung Trinh, the chief medical officer at Healthy Brain Clinic in Long Beach, California, it’s probably too soon to pop open the champagne (or brew a celebratory pot) over the potential perks of your coffee habit.

“It’s far too early to treat coffee—or caffeic acid—as an anti-aging intervention,” Trinh tells Popular Science.

Industry observers note that despite its inconsistent status as a health food, coffee has been consistently linked to longer life and a lower likelihood of certain diseases, though it’s not certain why. The Texas A&M study, led by Dr. Stephen Safe, focused on a cellular receptor called NR4A1.

NR4A1 is a protein that regulates how cells respond to stress and damage. The study found that several compounds in coffee, particularly polyphenols—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—bind to the NR4A1 receptor. One of these polyphenols, caffeic acid, is found in coffee and many other plants and, despite its name, has nothing to do with caffeine. These compounds seem to promote NR4A1’s protective effects, including mitigating cellular damage and slowing the growth of cancer cell line in laboratory models.

Industry observers note that in other words, the harder your NR4A1 proteins are working, the better your cells may be at fending off damage. Sign me up!

After researchers removed NR4A1 from cells in the lab, those benefits stopped, suggesting this receptor may help produce them. So, if coffee really helps NR4A1 do its job, we might just have a new anti-aging drink on our hands.

Interestingly, caffeine does not appear to play a key part in this mechanism, Trinh indicates. Instead, those benefits seem to come from coffee’s other compounds, like caffeic acid and its fellow polyphenols.

“What stood out to me was that the story was not really about caffeine,” he says. “I also found it interesting that the researchers did more than simply show that these compounds could bind to the receptor—they demonstrated NR4A1-dependent effects in cells. That makes the mechanism more compelling.”.

Translation: The study didn’t just show that coffee compounds attach to NR4A1; it revealed that this binding actually seems to activate the protein’s protective effects.

Consistent with this, the study also found that decaf coffee demonstrated similar protective effects on the lab cells, providing further evidence that coffee’s benefits may not have anything to do with caffeine at all.

“One of the interesting messages from this paper is that coffee should not be thought of as simply a delivery system for caffeine,” Trinh states. “Caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, ferulic acid, and several other coffee compounds all interacted with NR4A1, while caffeine showed much more variable NR4A1-related activity.”.

So, coffee’s superpower might not come from caffeine at all, at least when it comes to anti-aging benefits.

Before you start guzzling triple lattes in the name of cellular protection, know that “more” does not always mean “better.”.

“We simply cannot infer from this study that more coffee means more NR4A1 benefit,” Trinh claims. This is because the researchers studied coffee extracts and purified compounds in a lab setting rather than giving human subjects increasing amounts of coffee and measuring NR4A1 activity. Plus, in human biology, it’s possible to have too much of a good thing, Trinh says.

In a recent development, “At some point, additional coffee can bring unwanted effects from caffeine, including sleep disruption, anxiety, palpitations, or increases in blood pressure in susceptible people,” he states. “Those effects could counteract other health benefits. So, this study should not be interpreted as establishing either an optimal number of cups or a dose-response relationship for this pathway.”.

Trinh adds that as compelling as the study’s findings are, he doesn’t yet believe they justify changing recommendations around coffee consumption.

Earlier studies have linked coffee drinking to living longer and to better outcomes for some age-related conditions, Trinh states. But those studies couldn’t explain why. This one offers “one possible biological explanation,” he says.

Like most early-stage research, Trinh notes, this study can’t be applied to humans sipping their morning “cup of ambition.” Much of the work used a specific cancer cell in the lab, along with mouse immune cells, rather than testing regular human coffee drinkers directly. And while the study identified a potentially promising mechanism, it’s not clear how this mechanism will translate to human health outcomes.

Ultimately, Trinh states, no single food or compound is likely to be the deciding factor in how well we age.

Recent findings suggest that for a coffee addict like myself, though, these findings are the best kind of wake-up call. Coffee may or may not turn back the clock, but it does stop me from hitting snooze 15 times.

“The much bigger determinants of healthy aging remain things such as regular physical activity, good sleep, avoiding smoking, controlling blood pressure and metabolic risk, maintaining social and cognitive engagement, and eating an overall nutritious diet,” Trinh notes.

“This study is a promising piece of the scientific puzzle, not a prescription for another cup of coffee.”.

The Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix is one of the most glamorous weekends in sports. With drivers’ global followings and a long list of A-listers in attendance, the event can feel as much like a fashion show as a race.

But while many guests were focused on the designer labels, Kristin Juszczyk had another message in mind: the need for more research on women in sports.

In a recent development, juszczyk is a self-taught designer whose work began as a hobby and has since made her a force in the industry. The wife of San Francisco 49ers player Kyle Juszczyk, her custom game-day outfits gained traction on social media, and she has gone on to dress high-profile names including Simone Biles, Taylor Swift, and Caitlin Clark. This year, she was also named to TIME’s 100 Most Influential People in Sports.

For the Las Vegas GP, Juszczyk partnered with Gatorade’s Body of Science, an initiative dedicated to advancing the research on women’s sports. One stat drives their research: 6 percent of sports science research focuses on women.

Only 6 percent of published research in sports and exercise journals has focused exclusively on women, per a study published in the Women in Sport and Physical Activity Journal—a staggering gap that has implications for everything from training to recovery, as previously reported by Women’s Health.

Tennis legend Venus Williams, a Gatorade athlete, wore a custom look Juszczyk designed for the paddock red carpet inspired by this staggering statistic.

“Venus is one of the most iconic athletes of our generation, and to have her being in one of my designs, is surreal,” Juszczyk exclusively tells Women’s Health.

She opted to use leather as the base material, feeling like it channeled the energy of the sport. From there, she designed a trench coat with a layering corset piece over it, an homage to the city’s glitz and glamour.

Designing a trench coat was a first for Juszczyk, but the corset design is what she describes as her personal “bread and butter.” True to the Gatorade brand, the trench featured piping in its iconic orange, offset with black.

That 6 percent statistic is also front and center, ensuring the message of the design is clear: There needs to be more research dedicated toward women’s sports.

It has been revealed that juszczyk wanted to stay true to Venus and her personal style, and did a lot of research on what she wears on the regular. She states she approaches all of her designs with intentionality, ensuring the client is wearing something they feel good in.

“I want it to feel like my design, but I still want it to be something they feel beautiful and confident in,” she states.

According to recent reports, the look was on full display when Venus presented the winner of the F1 Academy race, Alisha Palmowski, with her trophy. The moment was symbolic: a titan of women’s sports celebrating the upcoming generation, while calling attention to a research gap that directly affects them.

“If anyone can take anything away from it, it’s that women need as much research in sports as men do,” she claims. “The world is doing so much in pushing women athletes forward, and science should back it as well.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT.
  • It has been revealed that "Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," indicates Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska.
  • Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT. Okay, maybe not everyone, but there's a reason yogurt has been a dietary staple in dozens of countries for centuries. Yogurt doesn't spoil as fast as milk, yet still delivers milk's nutrients—protein, calcium, potassium, magnesium—without the same risk of, um, certain GI problems.

It has been revealed that "Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," indicates Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska. "Humans figured out that even if they were lactose intolerant, they could still consume cultured milks because the culture helps degrade the lactose before it gets to the colon and gets fermented by gas-producing microbes.".

Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.

Recent findings suggest that from Europe to Asia to Africa, all yogurt starts with the same basic ingredients: milk and good bacteria. But no two types are exactly alike. Here's what to know before your next grocery run.

Recent findings suggest that traditional Greek yogurt is strained through a cheesecloth to remove excess fluid. Yogurt factories use centrifuges or special filters instead. What's left behind is a thick, smooth yogurt with a slightly acidic flavor and a concentrated source of nutrients, including about 18 grams of protein per 6-ounce container.

Some food makers add thickeners as a shortcut, so check the label for a simple ingredient list of milk, cream, and yogurt cultures. "The products with thickeners added have a different texture, a little bit more gumminess," states Molly Kimball, RD, CSSD, a dietitian based in Louisiana. Swap in Greek yogurt for sour cream or mayo, or stir it into guacamole—the lactic acid slows down the oxidation that turns avocados brown.

Sources indicate that technically considered a soft cheese, skyr is strained like Greek yogurt to produce something firm yet creamy. It's usually made with skim milk, yielding yogurt with slightly more protein than Greek yogurt: about 19 grams of protein per 6 ounces. Use skyr to make dips hearty enough to stand up to cut vegetables (or chips). Or stir it into bolognese to impart a velvety texture and an extra boost of protein.

This yogurt variety isn't strained, so it has a thinner texture and less protein than its Greek or Icelandic cousins: about 6 grams per 6 ounces. Traditional Bulgarian yogurt gets its signature sharp flavor from high concentrations of the aptly named Lactobacillus Bulgaricus bacteria, which produce lactic acid. Kimball recommends blending Bulgarian yogurt into smoothies to add a tanginess that counterbalances sweeter ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that most yogurts are fermented in large vats. As yogurt bacteria digest milk, they produce a wide variety of metabolites, including gel-like substances called exopolysaccharides. Then the yogurt is pumped into the smaller containers we snag at the grocery store.

With French-style yogurt, the milk and bacterial cultures are poured into cups earlier, before the microbes multiply. "That gives you a more custardy product because it hasn't gone through this pumping phase that disturbs the gel," says Hutkins. Inside a 6-ounce cup of French-style yogurt, you'll find about 5 grams of protein. To try it the French way, eat your yogurt for dessert, alone or paired with a little honey or jam.

According to recent reports, this tangy, thin, pourable yogurt is fermented with kefir grains–gelatinous clusters that contain milk proteins and up to 50 bacterial and yeast species. During fermentation, these yeasts can leave behind traces of alcohol and carbon dioxide, or fizz. However, many mass-produced kefirs use standardized starter cultures instead to maintain consistent product quality and keep the alcohol concentration low enough to sell in grocery stores.

Recent findings suggest that kimball suggests drinking plain kefir, Russian or otherwise. It packs about 8 grams of protein per cup. If you can't handle the sour flavor, balance it with a teaspoon or less of maple syrup or a few drops of stevia or monk fruit. If you want a flavored variety, pick one with no more than 5 grams of added sugar.

It has been revealed that sweet and mildly acidic, dahi is the key ingredient in Indian staples like lassi–a yogurt drink often flavored with mango, spices, or rosewater–and raita, the sauce that cools your mouth when you order your vindaloo extra hot. Some dahi varieties contain Leuconostoc, bacteria that produce a metabolite called diacetyl that imparts a buttery flavor. Each six-ounce serving of dahi packs about 7 grams of protein.

Drinkable like kefir, laban is sour but smooth and contains about 5 grams of protein per six ounces. Strain it in a colander or cheesecloth to make labneh, a thick, soft, yogurt-like cheese traditionally smeared on sandwiches and stacked on mezze platters.

This drinkable yogurt is often thicker than fermented milk beverages. Its mix of cultures, which hail mostly from the Lactobacillusgenus, imparts a moderately acidic flavor with subtle buttery notes. Amasi packs about 6 grams of protein per six ounces. It's traditionally eaten with maize or sorghum porridge, especially at breakfast.

Julie Stewart is a writer and content strategist whose work has also appeared in Health, and Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Vice, and Shape.

💡 Key Takeaways
