  • In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.
  • Toyota initially stated about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially stated about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

According to recent reports, the glitch stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota remarked the concern occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota said in the NHTSA report that the glitch was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

Industry observers note that OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Recent findings suggest that other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet confirmed next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

Recent findings suggest that even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

“Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”.

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

In a recent development, the largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Miami is a hotbed for avant-garde fashion, design, and art, which is why people flock to the tip of the Florida peninsula every year to navigate the crowds at events like the upcoming Art Basel Festival and Design Miami. History buffs can explore architecture from the 1920s at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, stroll the Deering Estate house museum, or study up on Miami’s urban and environmental design at the Coral Gables Museum. There’s plenty of nightlife to speak of, too, but if you’re aiming for something more low-key, catch a live performance at the Historic Miracle Theatre, or head over to ArtecHouse Miami to immerse yourself in interactive art.

In a recent development, you could even devote a day or so to scouring the food scene. May we suggest a Cuban food tour of Little Havana or noshing at trendy spots like the playful, pastel-hued Casadonna? Local favorites like the News Cafe, the historic restaurant where Gianni Versace used to venture to pick up his daily newspaper, and newer openings like cocktail bar Little Torch, with its Golden Milk Punch, are not to be overlooked as well.

Just know whether you’re traveling solo or going in with a group, there are countless Miami airbnbs to set you up for an epic trip to remember. The stays we found include a tranquil paradise with a private saltwater pool, a contemporary high-rise condo downtown, and an Art Deco-style suite a stone’s throw from Biscayne Bay. Throughout the space, a restrained palette and clean-lined furnishings draw inspiration from Japanese minimalism. A tatami-style dining table, low platform beds, and a concrete bathroom with wood-beamed ceilings make additional ornamentation superfluous. Perks: Open proposal layout, outdoor patio, modern design.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (536 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Hackers use old Bitly links to re-direct to offensive content

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media.
  • That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.
  • Sources indicate that link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media. According to the service provider Bitly, its hyperlinks in older tweets from many companies, politicians, and even government accounts are now redirecting to “content unrelated to the original posts.”.

That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.

Sources indicate that link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds. The service typically works by pinning a website’s lengthy, complex URL address to a tidied-up, abbreviated shortcut in a digital registry. This shortened address then redirects anyone who clicks it to their intended online destination.

Well…in theory. Security analysts have tried to warn people about an concern known as “bit rot” for decades. In 2009—about one year after Bitly’s debut—Silicon Valley entrepreneur Joshua Schacter wrote a prescient blog post cautioning against what he felt were potentially serious flaws in the link-shortening “middleman” system. Amid the concerns, Schacter cited a “latest and potentially unreliable” tool that ties an original hyperlink to the “health of a third party.”.

Sources indicate that “The shortener may decide a link is a Terms Of Service violation and delete it. If the shortener accidentally erases a database, forgets to renew its domain, or just disappears, the link will break,” he explained. “If a top-level domain changes its policy on commercial use, the link will break. If the shortener gets hacked, every link becomes a potential phishing attack.”.

It now appears bad actors recently identified countless of these Bitly links previously posted across social media between 2009 and 2014. Although their exact methods aren’t clear, it’s possible they generated their own custom Bitly links using the addresses in the social media posts, then used those to send people to different destinations. Bitly says its links do not automatically expire, but paid people may redirect existing links.

Sources indicate that many examples were found among the more than 60,000 posts on X from President Donald Trump’s official account. In one of Trump’s previous posts about his golf course in Scotland, the Bitly link temporarily redirected to Wikipedia’s entry on the Epstein Files. Targets also included corporations like McDonald’s, with one of the fast food giant’s 2011 Bitly URLs suddenly linked to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

Recent findings suggest that not every hijacked post funneled people to upsetting outcomes. Instead of a cybersecurity PSA, the Bitly address in a 2021 post from the FBI briefly linked to a photo of a blubbery seal. Another of Trump’s URLs sent you to the popular video game, Geometry Dash.

In its acknowledgement of the problem on November 15, Bitly reported it had identified and suspended the bad actors’ accounts, and were in the process of “disabling the affected links.”.

“Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the matter and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote at the time.

The 21 Best Adam Driver Movies, Ranked

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LET’S SWIFTLY CUT to the chase: Adam Driver is a good actor.
  • Some may still think of Driver, who this month teams up with director James Gray for one of his best roles ever in the crime drama Paper Tiger, as Adam Sackler, the overly emotional Brooklyn boyfriend of Lena Dunham in Girls (a role for which he was nominated for three Emmys).
  • It has been revealed that driver has emerged in recent years as someone who works almost exclusively with elite, top-notch directors, headlining projects from the likes of Scorsese and Michael Mann as well as Spike Lee and Ridley Scott (just to name a few).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LET’S SWIFTLY CUT to the chase: Adam Driver is a good actor. That’s probably an understatement to say the least; if Martin Scorsese, of all people, refers to someone as “one of the finest, if not the finest actor of his generation,” well, then, yeah, they’re probably pretty good.

Some may still think of Driver, who this month teams up with director James Gray for one of his best roles ever in the crime drama Paper Tiger, as Adam Sackler, the overly emotional Brooklyn boyfriend of Lena Dunham in Girls (a role for which he was nominated for three Emmys). But while he was obviously stellar in his breakthrough role on HBO’s hit comedy, it’s clear that he’s come a significant way in the time since first coming through to the public consciousness.

It has been revealed that driver has emerged in recent years as someone who works almost exclusively with elite, top-notch directors, headlining projects from the likes of Scorsese and Michael Mann as well as Spike Lee and Ridley Scott (just to name a few). He frequently reveals his comedy (or, maybe dramedy) chops working with Noah Baumbach.

He’s also, of course, earned his presence on the blockbuster scene: while opinions abound with regard to the Star Wars sequel trilogy, it’d be hard for anyone to deny the intensity with which Driver dominates the screen as the main villain of those films.

Industry observers note that for someone whose film career has only been going for about a decade, Driver has a remarkable resume and, having been nominated for a pair of Oscars already, accomplished a huge amount. As he continues to add more and more exciting projects to his ledger—he’s recently joined the cast of Marvel’s latest X-Men movie— we wanted to rank the very best roles Driver has had so far.

Here are the best films of Adam Driver, ranked.

In one of his first leading roles, Driver gave audiences a taste of the intense leading man he would eventually become as one half of a deeply troubled couple (with a newborn child) in Hungry Hearts.

One thing we haven’t gotten enough of—in the post-Girls era—is Driver showing off his full comedy chops. In What If, a rom-com where he stars alongside Daniel Radcliffe, Zoe Kazan, and Mackenzie Davis, he gets to have a whole lot of fun as a romantic co-lead (and yell about having sex and eating nachos).

Recent findings suggest that white Noise marked Driver’s fifth collaboration with writer/director Noah Baumbach. And while the movie didn’t wind up getting the Oscar love that it may have aspired for, it still found Driver giving a committed and intense—if deeply strange—performance. Fans of Don DeLillo's book upon which the film is based probably enjoyed what he brought to the table here.

According to recent reports, one of the hallmarks of Driver’s recent career is working with as many legendary directors as he can possibly fit into his schedule. That includes three movies with indie king Jim Jarmusch; Father Mother Sister Brother cast Driver as a key piece of a striking ensemble, and delivered one of his most naturalistic and honest recent performances.

Speaking of legendary directors, Driver took the lead in Megalopolis, the maximalist, long-in-the-works sci-fi epic from Francis Ford Coppola (of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now fame), as an urban planner or architect of some sort in a bizarre future world. The movie is kind of a massive disaster, but Driver, as always, brings his all (with some legendary line-readings included). It’s hard to say it’s good, but you certainly can’t look away—and it’s clearly an experience Driver wanted. An important touchstone for his career in any regard.

It has been revealed that megalopolis is not streaming anywhere or available on physical media. You are on your own with this one—if you find it, let me know.

In a movie full of larger-than-life, outrageous characters (and even more outrageous accents), Driver manages to somewhat keep House of Gucci on the rails. He plays Ridley Scott’s Maurizio Gucci, and while he, too, has an absurd accent, it somehow winds up being the most grounded and reasoned performance in the whole film. This movie is camp, but Driver winds up playing it pretty straight—which mostly works.

Driver’s first collaboration with Noah Baumbach came as Lev, a dude who comes in and out of the life of Greta Gerwig’s titular character as she flails her way through her 20s. This light and fun character feels almost like the opposite of Driver’s intense turn in another coming-of-age-in-NYC-story, Girls.

In The Report, Driver plays Daniel Jones, the real-life investigator who led the search into the CIA’s use of torture in the aftermath of 9/11. This gripping true story isn’t one of Driver’s flashiest performances, but it may be his most pertinent to the world we live in today.

Industry observers note that driver made his first—and so far only—appearance in a Coen Brothers film with an ever-so-brief couple of scenes as Al Cody in Inside Llewyn Davis. He makes himself known in those scenes, though, as a gimmicky country music cowboy whose sole job is to say things like “OUUUUTER….. SPAAACEEEEE” on songs intended to be cheap radio hits. Still, Driver gives this character a sense of humanity in offering the titular musician (Oscar Isaac) a place to stay. He’s out of the movie just about as quickly as he gets into it, but it’s the definition of a scene-stealing turn.

According to recent reports, this movie is weird! Driver plays a problematic stand-up comedian named Henry McHenry (that’s right) who’s married to an opera singer (Marion Cotillard)... and then they have a daughter, who is… a wunderkind musician, and also a marionette puppet. Things go way off the rails from there in a way that we wouldn’t dare spoil, but trust us on this: it’s pretty easily the most bonkers movie on this list.

There’s not much to Paterson—a film about a bus driver who writes poetry—but it’s one of Driver’s most unique and subdued performances, quite the shift for a guy so well known for going massive and intense.

To play a Jesuit monk in Silence, Martin Scorsese’s long-gestating (but little-seen) 2016 passion project, Driver went full Method, losing nearly 50 pounds in preparation to play the role (according to co-star Andrew Garfield during an interview on The Late Show). This reflects on Driver’s performance, where he’s as intense and dialed in as he’s ever been.

Recent findings suggest that by teaming up with the legendary Michael Mann (Heat, Collateral, Miami Vice), Driver manages to check yet another iconic director off his list. In this slow burn, brooding drama, Driver plays Enzo Ferrari, a win-at-all-costs businessman and racing team leader who finds himself, in 1957, at a crossroads with regards to both his troubled business and complicated personal/family life. Driver gives a subdued performance that scorches through the screen as the viewer constantly wonders whether he’s pushed one part of his life too far; he gives an Italian accent once again, by the way, and it goes a lot better than it did in House of Gucci.

Driver totally pops in While We’re Young, his second collab with Noah Baumbach. Here, he plays an ambitious and opportunistic Bushwick hipster who, along with his wife (Amanda Seyfried) meets an older couple (Ben Stiller and Naomi Watts) and become their “cool” friends. This movie is a very funny commentary on friendship, careers, and being content with getting older—and Driver’s character (a wannabe documentarian who doesn’t seem to have any sort of moral or ethical code) is a huge highlight.

Sources indicate that rian Johnson brought Kylo Ren to the brink in Star Wars: The Last Jedi, giving Driver’s striking, and, at times, maniacal villain the chance to really set himself apart from others in the franchise. The movie dives into Kylo’s relationship with all sorts of characters, including Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) and Rey (Daisy Ridley), leading to an epic film-ending interaction with the former—and tons of confused fans online wishing he would get together with the latter. The movie leaves Ren in a position where he could have potentially become the most evil and powerful villain the series has ever seen; unfortunately, The Rise of Skywalker squandered all of it.

Recent findings suggest that imagine Steven Soderbergh’s Logan Lucky as the blue-collar version of his Ocean’s trilogy. Driver plays a war veteran bartender (who lost his forearm during a tour of duty) who, along with his brother (Channing Tatum) stage a major heist at a NASCAR racetrack. Driver plays his character as slow, but not a complete idiot—because this movie is far too smart for such 2-D characterizations. An extremely fun movie with a stacked cast.

Teaming up with writer/director Spike Lee to play undercover detective Philip "Flip" Zimmerman in BlacKkKlansman earned Driver his first Oscar nomination, something that even at the time felt overdue—but was very, very deserved. This movie plays strongly on the relationship between Driver and John David Washington, and finds Driver playing, essentially, two characters: his noble detective, and the person he has to become while infiltrating the KKK.

Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of actors out there who reach a certain level of fame and get a little skittish when it comes to playing characters who could even potentially be seen as unsavory. In The Last Duel, Driver gives an absolutely fearless performance as Jacques Le Gris, a 14th-century knight who’s not only unsavory, but absolutely vile. The charm that we’ve gotten so frequently from Driver works to perfection here, as a character who at first invites an air of indifference eventually becomes so disgusting that he’s without question the worse of two evils. The Last Duel spends the duration of its running time asking questions about the truth and how it evolves over time—and while the specifics may be uncertain, the movie makes no mistakes about how heinous this character is (and how perfectly despicable Driver plays him).

Sources indicate that marriage Story brought Driver his second (and most recent) Oscar nomination, and a tidal wave of online memes (you’ve almost certainly seen him punch that wall more times than you’ve actually seen the movie), but his fourth collaboration with Noah Baumbach is probably his most impressive dramatic performance to date. Telling the male side of a dissolved relationship (Scarlett Johansson plays his soon-to-be-ex-wife), Driver finds the perfect mix of charming, charismatic, and delusional in playing Charlie, the man at (one half of) the center of the story.

After 2022’s Armageddon Time, James Gray had another largely autobiographical story to tell in Paper Tiger, this time more in line with his origins as a teller of crime drama stories. While Paper Tiger once again features characters based on Gray’s parents (this time Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson, after they were played by Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway in Armageddon Time), it adds a new character named Uncle Gary to the mix, played by Driver. Gary is a brash, lovable former cop, an ambitious businessman who goes around town like he owns the place and brings fancy dinners (shout out Peter Luger!) into his family’s home as a special surprise when he’s got a deal to spring on his brother. Of course, these kinds of deals in movies are never as good as they seem, and everyone winds up in more trouble than they bargained for. Driver plays the character in a gray area, and his plethora of charisma make it one of his very best roles to date. When he’s on screen, you simply can’t look away.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Industry observers note that texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

In a recent development, utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of newly introduced capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” mentioned Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

Sources indicate that the US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Recent findings suggest that solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

In a recent development, you wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

The article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

The storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

Recent findings suggest that more than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty indicates the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

In a recent development, on November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce stated in a statement.

The Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

Sources indicate that “The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization remarked. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.

At its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell. It also includes cognitive health—your ability to think, learn, and remember.

Recent findings suggest that because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it. Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease can begin about 20 years before symptoms appear, making a proactive approach to brain health an important part of caring for your overall health.

In a recent development, this messaging inspired actress, author, and advocate Julianne Moore to partner with Eli Lilly and Company on their Brain Health Matters campaign to encourage people to prioritize their brain health. “From my conversations with people living with Alzheimer’s disease, I’ve seen how much proactive care matters,” Moore states. “That’s why I’m helping to encourage everyone to prioritize their brain health through regular conversations with their doctors.”.

According to recent reports, not sure where to begin? Here are five ways to make brain health a priority part in your overall health.

You might not have any concerns about cognitive decline, much less dementia. But taking a proactive approach to cognitive health doesn’t have to wait until later in life—or until something feels off. One brain change associated with Alzheimer’s disease involves amyloid, a protein the body produces naturally. Talking to your doctor can help you understand your personal risk factors and discuss whether steps such as establishing a cognitive baseline and adopting brain-healthy habits may be appropriate for you.

In a recent development, add brain health to your “must-ask” list for medical appointments and come prepared with specific questions to guide the conversation. Ask your doctor whether a cognitive assessment is appropriate for you. This spoken, written, or digital evaluation can provide a starting point for monitoring your memory and thinking over time.

While a cognitive assessment cannot diagnose a condition on its own, establishing a baseline and completing follow-up assessments as recommended by your doctor may help spot early signs of memory and thinking challenges and monitor changes over time.

Here’s what you may want to ask your doctor:.

Recent findings suggest that research shows that up to 45 percent of dementia cases, including those caused by Alzheimer’s disease, may be prevented or delayed by managing changeable risk factors. These include blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; lifestyle habits around diet, exercise, alcohol consumption, and smoking; and even hearing loss, depression, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and sleep.

You can’t change everything that affects your risk—such as age, family history, or certain genetic markers. But your doctor can help you understand the risk factors that may apply to you and build a blueprint to manage those that can be changed. The following brain-healthy habits can be a good place to start:.

Industry observers note that once you understand your risk factors, establish a cognitive baseline, and identify brain-healthy habits that could work for you, the next step is bringing those pieces together. Work with your doctor to create a plan based on your individual health needs.

In a recent development, your blueprint might include ways to manage changeable risk factors, behaviors that support your brain health, and a schedule for revisiting your cognitive health with your doctor. Regular conversations with your doctor about these topics can help you take action early and help support your brain health for the future.

Honest discussions around brain health can help go a long way toward reducing stigma and helping others feel more comfortable seeking information, support, and care. Opening up—even in small ways—can make a difference, whether you’re checking in with loved ones, sharing your own concerns, or simply normalizing the topic in everyday life.

According to recent reports, “Brain health is something we don’t talk about often enough,” Moore says. “There’s so much fear around cognitive health and even talking to a doctor about getting an assessment. I think it needs to be normalized.”.

To learn more about how you can be proactive for your brain health, visit BrainHealthMatters.com.

#134040. Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

📅 25 May 2022 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1266 w)

Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

📅 25 May 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, if you listen to the supplement industry, no, not really.
  • Industry observers note that N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years.
  • That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IS THERE ANYTHING NAC can’t do? Well, if you listen to the supplement industry, no, not really.

Industry observers note that N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years. Depending on who you listen to, NAC supplements can allegedly boost your immune system, detoxify your body, improve cognitive function, increase energy levels, slow aging, increase fertility, reduce inflammation, prevent respiratory infections, and decrease oxidative stress.

That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.

Add that to the fact that NAC is a proven medical treatment for a couple of specific diagnoses, and you have the perfect setup. Supplement companies can extrapolate evidence into claims that go way beyond current scientific evidence. That’s been a blessing and a curse for NAC manufacturers—and a legal headache that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) just made a major move to solve with the proposed creation of a upcoming regulatory category just for NAC.

In a recent development, the legal maneuvering is complicated and, if finalized, would allow NAC to be considered a supplement but still a medical treatment which technically isn’t allowed—yet. Basically, there’s a lot to unpack here.

Industry observers note that so what can NAC supplement do? And what even is NAC? Is it safe? Let’s break it all down.

Recent findings suggest that NAC IS A sulfur-containing compound, a precursor of the amino acid L-cysteine. In medicinal or supplement form, NAC is converted directly into cysteine, which is then used to make and deliver glutathione, a powerful antioxidant that the body uses to scavenge free radicals and manage oxidative stress. (Yes, the body is a complex system.).

While NAC isn’t found in food, cysteine is readily available in animal proteins, legumes, dairy, nuts and seeds, and some vegetables. Compared to dietary cysteine, NAC supplements are a faster, more stable way of increasing glutathione levels.

It has been revealed that NAC supplements are available in powders, capsules, liquids, and tablets. And while NAC has legitimate medical uses, it’s not officially FDA-approved as a supplement as of this second. Of course, this hasn’t stopped the supplement industry from selling it—or influencers from promoting it.

In a recent development, NAC has been in a weird legal gray area for years. Because it’s an actual medical treatment, it technically can’t be classified as a supplement, even though it’s often presented that way.

Industry observers note that the FDA’s proposed rule would classify NAC as the first-ever “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition.” Basically, it will be allowed to span the categories of supplement and medication, which has never been done before. If finalized, this ruling would “provide for the lawful use of certain ingredients in dietary supplements that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition,” per an FDA constituent upgrade.

In a recent development, the proposed rule would allow products that contain NAC to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, as long as they’re not otherwise in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). In theory, this may eventually apply to other supplement-ish ingredients; Right now, this is centered around NAC.

The proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days. It’s not clear when the FDA when glitch a final rule.

According to recent reports, this won’t really impact the general public if it’s finalized. Instead, it clears up potential legal problems surrounding NAC. “This will more formally allow sales of NAC over the counter, without a prescription,” states Jamie Alan, PharmD, PhD, a professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University in East Lansing.

While some members of the MAHA movement have pushed for this, Alan says it’s also a case of “well, why not.” She explains, “It is generally safe, and I agree with that assessment. It is also being sold as a supplement already so, why not?”.

It has been revealed that alan stresses that this move doesn’t suddenly legitimize all NAC supplements or claims surrounding them. “If you are buying a supplement, you aren’t necessarily guaranteed that the bottle contains what it notes it does,” she says. “There really isn’t evidence yet in my opinion that supplementing with NAC as a dietary supplement will be life-changing for the vast majority of people.”.

In a recent development, NAC is the standard treatment for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose. High levels of acetaminophen deplete the liver of glutathione, which is required for the body’s detox pathways. If you’re curious about the geeky scientific mechanism: Swiftly repleting glutathione by way of an intravenous NAC infusion helps clear the excess metabolites from the overdose and prevent liver damage.

Industry observers note that NAC is also a mucolytic, meaning it can break down thick mucus in the respiratory system. (Yum.) While recent research found that NAC may help with with COPD and chronic bronchitis feel less worse, more investigation is needed to clearly establish effects and benefits.

WELL, NOT ALL that much. Other scientific trials have looked at NAC’s effects on conditions including mood and compulsive disorders, Alzheimer’s, Schizophrenia, and chronic pain. Overall, results have been mixed and largely unremarkable. For most of these conditions and disorders, larger-scale clinical trials are still needed.

So while it’s true that research does exist on NAC and wider health benefits, most of the upcoming research trials examining NAC’s effects use doses that are far higher than what the average person would take, and in forms that are not available to the public.

This hasn’t stopped wellness influencers from broadcasting that NAC supplements can help heal whatever ails you.

Many of these influencers argue that because glutathione may reduce oxidative stress, NAC is amazing for longevity and anti-aging. It’s simple, they argue: Because oxidative stress is associated with aging, increasing glutathione with NAC supplements slows biological aging.

It has been revealed that except raising levels of glutathione in the body does not necessarily translate into a desired outcome. Science agrees: There is no long-term human evidence that showing that this suppresses oxidative stress to the level of having a clinically meaningful outcome. Taking NAC for “healthy aging” is more marketing than anything else at this point.

Industry observers note that FOR MOST HEALTHY people, NAC supplements appear to be safe in doses between 600 milligrams (mg) to 1800mg per day. However, doses on the higher end of that range may have a higher risk of side effects such as gastrointestinal upset.

According to recent reports, NAC is not recommended for people with clotting disorders. There are also some potential drug interactions between NAC and immunosuppressants, so it’s always a good idea to get a doctor or pharmacist to cross-reference any supplements with the medications you’re taking.

It has been revealed that again, remember that the supplement industry is largely unregulated. Always buy from reputable companies, and look for products that are third-party tested to ensure that what’s on the label is actually what’s in the bottle.

NAC has some legitimate—and even life-saving—medical uses, and research is constantly evolving. But what the supplements don’t have at this point, is compelling human evidence showing that NAC has any clinically meaningful effects in healthy people.

In a recent development, the Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

Protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Industry observers note that researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he said, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

Sources indicate that an Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

According to recent reports, axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Sources indicate that the plan replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how owners authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage at the moment sits.

According to recent reports, wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

Bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

So the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. Now we wait on action, and more assurances that crypto is safe from AI threats. Assurances that could ensure the bottom is in fact in, if and when they arrive….

It has been revealed that when it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

It has been revealed that and that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

Sources indicate that there are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

Sources indicate that carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, indicates Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

It has been revealed that fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a substantial role in satiety, White states. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—notable at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

The brand’s midcentury-inspired dressers and nightstands are perennial favorites, but we’re particularly interested in the Shelter Sleeper sofa for anyone expecting out-of-town guests this holiday season. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert tested the queen-size version in dark olive performance velvet and called it “the softest, cushiest couch in my house.” Another standout from the sale is the midcentury five-drawer dresser, a handsome storage solution narrow enough for smaller bedrooms and cozy apartments. Equally impressive deals can be found on accent chairs, dining tables, and some of the brand’s bestsellers.

Pottery Barn’s extensive selection of living room, dining room, and bedroom furniture has earned it a reputation as a one-stop shop for furnishing an entire space. Its current Fall Sale includes up to 70% of select furniture, with additional discounts on certain styles. The brand is known for its comfortable, traditional seating, including the York Slope Arm Deep Seat Slipcovered Side Sleeper, presently 20% off. Contributor Kate McGregor tested the sofa and praised its plush cushions, washable slipcover, and easy-to-use sleeper mechanism. “This is one of the most comfortable sofas I’ve had the pleasure of sitting on,” she wrote. If your living room doubles as your guest room, this is one deal you won’t want to skip.

It has been revealed that it’s rare that a sofa is so versatile that it can adapt to a newly introduced apartment, growing household, or an entirely different floor plan, but not at Burrow. The direct-to-consumer furniture brand is already hosting a Black Friday Preview with up to 40% off. Its modular seating arrives in manageable sections that can be easily rearranged or expanded as your needs change. Contributor David Kaufman tested the Range three-piece open sectional lounger, which he described as a “crowd-pleaser in the house.” The Nomad leather sofa with ottoman is equally tempting, especially if a more tailored take is more your speed.

Perusing Nickey Kehoe’s sale section is akin to sifting through buried treasure. The Los Angeles design studio and retailer is known for furniture that feels thoughtful, rich with character, and difficult to pin to any one decorating era. Its Last Chance section offers up to 30% off distinctive pieces like the architectural Iron Canopy Bed and the Community Harvest Bench. Both have the kind of lived-in appeal that makes a room look as though it’s been furnished gradually, with pieces collected over time.

If your home office has been getting by with a less-than-ideal setup, Haworth’s current sale is a good reason to treat yourself. The office furniture specialist is currently offering 25% off select performance seating, desks, gaming furniture, lighting, and accessories, with ergonomic favorites like the Fern, Zody, and Soji chairs among its most popular pieces. But, the sale extends beyond seating. The Market Wire Frame Desk offers an industrial-leaning alternative to a conventional writing table, and the Elements Laminate Flare Leg Desk brings a cleaner, more minimalist silhouette to the workspace. Considering how much time we spend at our desks, a workspace that looks as good as it works hardly seems like an unreasonable indulgence.

#134026. Breaking: Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2155 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin isn't a shiny latest technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.
  • Recent findings suggest that the 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash.
  • We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin isn't a shiny latest technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

Recent findings suggest that the 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone reveals, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

Recent findings suggest that the adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

Sources indicate that the road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

Industry observers note that this progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

It has been revealed that one case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured major personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the newly introduced, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too major to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Recent findings suggest that much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

According to recent reports, people investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire organization is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the latest cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Recent findings suggest that third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news reveals. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

Industry observers note that A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Sources: Bitcoin, Mastercard, PayPal.

It has been revealed that bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

It has been revealed that you know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building fresh financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

According to recent reports, what we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous upcoming things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

In a recent development, even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a latest one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉.

Industry observers note that when it comes to mountain towns, there’s good, there’s great, and then there’s Aspen—so needless to say, Aspen’s hotels are the height of luxury. Among one of the world’s finest ski towns (with a whopping four mountains on one lift ticket), this winter wonderland is rife with dazzling accommodations. The best hotels in Aspen offer everything: luxury spa experiences; fine dining; ski-in, ski-out access; and all the après-ski cocktails you can get your hands on.

If resort life isn’t quite your speed, fear not—there are plenty of picture-perfect rentals you can snag on Airbnb or Vrbo. Expect a robust selection of spacious condominiums, luxury mountain chalets, and backcountry cabins, most of which are within walking distance from one of Snowmass or Aspen Mountain’s peak-reaching gondolas and ski resorts.

Don’t love the snow? Good thing Aspen is a top-tier year-round destination. Ideal for climbers, equestrians, cyclists, and other adventure-seekers, the Rocky Mountains provide a backdrop for just about any summertime alpine experience you can dream up. The town’s famed Food & Wine Classic in June is also a can’t miss. Each luxury hotel and off-the-beaten-path rental we found offers access to some of the best adventures in the West, whether you visit in January, July, or anytime in between. Consider this your cue to scroll below and book your stay while date availability lasts.

Perks: Daily champagne sabering, full-service spa, heated outdoor pool, multiple on-site restaurants, pet-friendly, valet parking.

Sources indicate that for the ultimate choice in old-school luxury, check in to the St. Regis. The grand, chalet-style property sits at the foot of Aspen Mountain—just a five-minute walk from the Silver Queen Gondola—and pairs classic Rocky Mountain charm with five-star hospitality. Inside, rooms are outfitted with buttery leather headboards, fine linens, marble bathrooms, and mountain views framed by mahogany trim, while the hotel’s on-call butler service can handle tasks like unpacking luggage and drawing a post-ski bath. The RAKxa Wellness Spa remains one of the best in town, offering oxygen facials, a heated outdoor pool (perfect for a post-slopes soak), and many more wellness-minded amenities. Still, this grande dame doesn’t take itself too seriously. Since 2023, it’s been home to The Snow Lodge, a winter spinoff of Montauk’s famed Surf Lodge. The après scene here has become the hottest ticket in Aspen—Diplo, Rampa, and Bob Moses have all spun sets in the open-air courtyard—while the group’s latest supper club and nightlife concept brings coastal-cool energy to the Rockies with candlelit dinners, Champagne towers, and late-night dancing under the stars. It’s a rare blend of heritage and hedonism—the kind of place where you can trade ski boots for stilettos without missing a beat. From $649 per night.

Perks: Fitness center, multiple restaurants and bars, in-town transport, heated pool and hot tubs, pet-friendly.

Perks: Ski-in/ski-out, heated outdoor pool, spa and fitness center, airport transfers, concierge desk, complimentary mini bar snacks and soft drinks.

According to recent reports, the only AAA Five Diamond–rated hotel in Aspen, the Little Nell blends the best of the West with the cosmopolitan luxuries you’d expect from a five-star hotel. Every detail is dialed in. Guests can unwind at the heated outdoor pool and hot tub, book a treatment at the Little Nell Spa, or rely on the property’s Les Clefs d’Or–certified concierge team, who have a reputation for making the impossible happen (heli-skiing trip to Telluride, anyone?). Food and wine take center stage here, too—the hotel’s Chefs & Somms dinners pair Michelin-caliber cuisine with rare vintages from a 20,000-bottle cellar, one of the most impressive in the Rockies. But it’s on the mountain where The Little Nell truly shines. The Ski Concierge team can arrange first tracks before the lifts open, snowcat powder tours, or private gear fittings in your room, ensuring you’re perfectly prepped with your helmet and bindings. From $800 per night.

Perks: Rooftop hot tub, lobby bar and restaurant, pet-friendly, EV charging.

For a quieter boutique experience, you’ll want to stay at Mollie Aspen. Opened in late 2023, the hotel blends Japanese and Scandinavian design, creating an atmosphere that feels immediately restorative. Roomy plush leather chairs, well-worn rugs, custom woodwork, and a plethora of unique design accents welcome weary travelers and exhausted skiers, exuding the type of vibe you’d expect from a well-loved and hard-to-reach mountain chalet. Despite the tucked-away vibe, Mollie’s location couldn’t be more central—you’re steps from downtown’s galleries, the Aspen Art Museum, and cultural landmarks like the Aspen Institute and Wheeler Opera House. If you’re too tired for a jaunt downtown, the Mollie also has a lobby restaurant and poolside rooftop bar where you can while away the hours. The rooftop, in particular, has become a gathering spot for the design-savvy après crowd, offering mountain views and mellow vinyl playlists. From $278 per night.

Perks: All-suite accommodations, outdoor heated lap pool and hot tub, fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, shuttle service.

Backed up against the Rocky Mountains, Aspen Meadows Resort is a midcentury masterpiece tailor-made for design aficionados. Originally conceived as part of the Aspen Institute campus by artist and architect Herbert Bayer, the property is steeped in Bauhaus principles, with clean lines, geometric forms, and a playful use of primary colors throughout its public and private spaces. Best for art and design nerds, the resort’s 98 suites feature Bauhaus-inspired furnishings, while common spaces include art exhibitions, outdoor sculptures, and West End Social, a recently redesigned restaurant with aspen-wood paneling, Colorado marble, and colorful textiles. Some of the stand-out amenities include a shuttle service with routes into town and the Aspen airport, a heated saline pool and hot tub, and ski butler service. When you’re looking to venture outside of the hotel’s chic walls, there are 40 acres to explore, which include plenty of great sledding hills for those visiting in the winter months and a massive sculpture collection. There’s also the on-site Resnick Center for Herbert Bayer Studies, where rotation exhibitions explore the artist’s legacy. With so much space for playing, there are more activities for visitors than could fit into 10 different trips. Can’t-miss itinerary items include themed scavenger hunts, hot-air balloon rides, fly fishing, snowshoeing, and—of course—lots of skiing. From $359 per night.

Perks: Airport shuttle, pet-friendly, on-site fitness room, rooftop lounge.

For travelers who want to be right in the heart of it all, The Limelight Hotel Aspen offers front-row access to the town’s best shops, restaurants, and bars—plus it’s just steps from the Silver Queen Gondola, which whisks skiers to the top of Aspen Mountain in under 20 minutes. The atmosphere is lively yet low-key, thanks to communal spaces like the buzzy lounge, where locals and visitors gather for wood-fired pizzas, live music, and craft cocktails. The property staff helps guests craft the perfect stay, with activities including hiking adventures, whitewater rafting, art museum visits, and more. Some rooms feature balconies and patios and are draped in mountain charm (think: wool blankets and fireplaces). From $299 per night.

Perks: Mountain view, wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit laundry, hot tub, security system, free parking, housekeeping available for a fee.

According to recent reports, just a block from the Silver Queen Gondola, this newly renovated two-bedroom condo makes it easy to spend mornings skiing Aspen Mountain and afternoons exploring the restaurants, boutiques, and après-ski spots in Aspen’s downtown area. Inside, cozy furnishings and a wood-burning fireplace make the living room an inviting place to warm up after a day on the slopes. The two bedrooms offer flexible sleeping arrangements, with a king bed in the primary suite and two twins that can be converted into another king in the second bedroom. The kitchen is outfitted with stainless steel appliances, an induction cooktop, and all the cooking equipment needed to whip up dinner at home, though with Ajax Tavern so close, you might not bother. From $865 per night.

Perks: Heated outdoor pool, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit laundry, pet-friendly, free parking.

Recent findings suggest that there is a lot of architectural woodwork to behold in this modern Aspen condo, but thanks to an abundance of windows, the effect reads bright and airy rather than moody ski lodge. Paneled ceilings, exposed timber rafters, wood floors, and floor-to-ceiling cabinetry bring plenty of warmth to the interiors, while clean-lined furnishings give the two-bedroom space a more contemporary feel. Equipped with one king bedroom and one queen, the condo is particularly well suited to two couples traveling together or a family of four. In the exteriors, the heated pool offers another way to unwind, though the slopes are hardly far away: The property sits just off the Lower Corkscrew run on Aspen Mountain, steps from Lift 1A. From $1,272 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, private patio, soaking tub, in-unit laundry, free parking, pet-friendly, housekeeping available for a fee.

Aspen's Victorian-era architecture is every bit as charming as its mountain scenery, and this one-bedroom apartment near Pioneer Park puts you in the middle of one of the town's most scenic historic neighborhoods. Recently remodeled, the 540-square-foot space has bright, sunlight interiors that includes an open-plan kitchen and living room that seems considerably larger thanks to oversized windows lining the walls. A queen bedroom separates guests from the main living area, and modern conveniences like air-conditioning, a dishwasher, and in-unit laundry make longer stays especially comfortable. Although the apartment sits on a peaceful residential street, downtown Aspen's restaurants, boutiques, and the historic Wheeler Opera House are just a short walk away, and a nearby bus stop makes getting to the ski slopes easy. From $391 per night.

Perks: Wrap-around deck, washer and dryer, wood burning fireplace, Wi-fi.

According to recent reports, tucked just behind the St. Regis, this one-bedroom apartment puts you right in the center of Aspen without feeling caught in the crowd. The interiors are warm and functional rather than flashy—a wood-burning fireplace, buttery cotton linens from Garnier-Thiebaut, and plenty of closet space for your suitcases give the space an easy, lived-in comfort. A wraparound deck nearly doubles the footprint, inviting morning coffee in the sun or an après-ski glass of wine with views of the surrounding peaks. Everything is set up to make a stay feel effortless. There’s dedicated parking, air conditioning, and in-unit laundry, plus a Sonos sound system and high-speed Wi-Fi for streaming or working remotely. The open kitchen has all the essentials, while the living room feels like a natural place to gather after a day outside. Professionally managed by Aspen Vacations, guests enjoy thoughtful extras—an invitation to the members-only Caribou Club, and insider tips on local dining and trail access are just a couple to name. Steps from world-class restaurants, boutiques, and the Silver Queen Gondola, this retreat feels equal parts modern pied-à-terre and alpine hideaway—a polished perch for soaking in the best of Aspen, no ski-valet required. From $408 per night.

Perks: Fireplace, free parking, washer and dryer, shared pool and hot tub.

Sources indicate that right on the edge of downtown Aspen, this riverfront condo feels worlds away from the bustle. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame the Roaring Fork River, filling the space with natural light and the sound of rushing water. Inside, the palette is crisp and minimal—soft grays, creamy whites, and natural wood—letting the view take center stage. The open living area flows onto a private balcony, and a sleek kitchen with stainless appliances and stone counters may convince you to eat in. Better yet, there’s some practical touches, like in-unit laundry and high-speed internet, as well as amenities more commonly seen in hotels, such as a shared indoor pool, hot tub, and gym. From $412 per night.

Industry observers note that craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.
